L14@P0: Abstract: Since the evolution of the electric and hybrid vehicle, the analysis of batteries’ characteristics
L15@P0: and influence on driving range has become essential. This fact advocates the necessity of accurate
L16@P0: simulation modeling for batteries. Different models for the Li-ion battery cell are reviewed in this
L17@P0: paper and a group of the highly dynamic models is selected for comparison. A new open circuit
L18@P0: voltage (OCV) model is proposed. The new model can simulate the OCV curves of lithium iron
L19@P0: magnesium phosphate (LiFeMgPO4) battery type at different temperatures. It also considers both
L20@P0: charging and discharging cases. The most remarkable features from different models, in addition
L21@P0: to the proposed OCV model, are integrated in a single hybrid electrical model. A lumped thermal
L22@P0: model is implemented to simulate the temperature development in the battery cell. The synthesized
L23@P0: electro-thermal battery cell model is extended to model a battery pack of an actual electric vehicle.
L24@P0: Experimental tests on the battery, as well as drive tests on the vehicle are performed. The proposed
L25@P0: model demonstrates a higher modeling accuracy, for the battery pack voltage, than the constituent
L26@P0: models under extreme maneuver drive tests.

L29@P0: 1. Introduction
L30@P0: The global climate change, escalation in fuel cost, and the energy consumption, urged the necessity
L31@P0: to replace the fossil fuel with renewable and environment friendly energy sources. Battery electric
L32@P0: vehicles (BEV) are one major application, demonstrating the replacement of fossil fuel by renewable
L33@P0: energy. Li-ion batteries have become the preferable energy storage for the future electric vehicles [1].
L34@P0: They receive greater attention than other battery types, such as lead-acid and nickel-cadmium batteries,
L35@P0: due to their practical physical characteristics. They have a high specific energy, specific power, power
L36@P0: density and a long life cycle. Moreover, their self-discharge rate is lower compared to other types of
L37@P0: batteries [1–3].

L106@P2: 2. Existing Battery Models
L107@P2: Different modeling approaches are found in the literature. The most prominent battery modeling
L108@P2: techniques are: Electrochemical, analytical, and circuit-based models [8]. Electrochemical models
L109@P2: employ non-linear differential equations to model the chemical and electrical behavior of the cell [4,9].
L110@P2: Detailed knowledge of the battery chemistry, material structure and other physical characteristics
L111@P2: are essential to achieve high accuracy and cover a large number of different operating points.
L112@P2: However, the producers of batteries will rarely reveal the full parameters set of their products.
L113@P2: Another shortcoming of electrochemical models is the high computational effort required to solve the
L114@P2: non-linear partial differential equations [8]. Electrochemical models are better suited for research in
L115@P2: battery’s components fabrication, like electrodes and electrolyte [4,10]. The analytical modeling, on the
L116@P2: other hand, reduces the computational complexity for the battery. However, that would be on the
L117@P2: expense of capturing the circuit physical features of the battery, such as open circuit voltage, output
L118@P2: voltage, internal resistance, and transient response [8].
L119@P2: Lumped electrical circuit models offer low complexity combined with high accuracy and
L120@P2: robustness in simulating batteries dynamics [11–13]. Models with single or double resistor-capacitor
L121@P2: (RC) networks are the best candidates for simulating the battery module [12–14]. RC parameters
L122@P2: employed to model the battery characteristic show a dependency on temperature, charge/discharge
L123@P2: rates and the SOC. Several techniques had been discussed in literature [1,15–19] for SOC estimation.
L124@P2: Lam and Bauer [20] proposed a circuit model for the Li-ion battery with variable open circuit
L125@P2: voltages, resistances and capacitances. The equivalent circuit components were represented as
L126@P2: empirical functions of the current direction, the SOC, the battery temperature and the C-rate.
L127@P2: Tremblay et al. [5,21] proposed an improved version Shepherd’s model [22]. This model considers the
L128@P2: influence of SOC on the OCV by considering the polarization voltage in the discharge-charge model.
L129@P2: Different dynamic models for Li-ion, lead-acid, NiMH and NiCd battery typed were presented in
L130@P2: Reference [5]. However, neither the temperature effect nor the variation of the internal resistance
L131@P2: were considered. Saw et al. [23] investigated the thermal behavior for a LiFePO4–graphite battery
L132@P2: by coupling the empirical equations of the modified Shephard’s battery model with a lumped
L133@P2: thermal model for the battery cell. The temperature development of a complete vehicle battery
L134@P2: pack under different driving cycles was simulated in [23]. Tan et al. [24] have incorporated the thermal
L135@P2: losses to Shephard’s model for Li-ion battery cells by adding temperature dependent correction
L136@P2: terms to the model. Wijewardana et al. [1] proposed a generic electro-thermal model for Li-ion
L137@P2: batteries. The model considers potential correction terms accounting for electrode film formation and
L138@P2: electrolyte electron transfer chemistry. In addition, the constant values in the empirical equations
L139@P2: that represent the equivalent circuit components of the battery were adjusted. These equations were
L140@P2: employed to model the electrical components in dependence of SOC and temperature. Wijewardana
L141@P2: et al. consider the C-rate effect in the estimation of SOC by employing an extended Kalman filter
L142@P2: technique. Computational thermal models and temperature distribution estimations were proposed
L143@P2: in References [25–28]. Additionally, finite element analysis models to estimate the temperature
L144@P2: distribution in the battery were presented in References [25,27–29]. This kind of simulation requires
L145@P2: knowledge of thermal properties of the battery cell materials, such as thermal capacity, density,
L146@P2: mechanical construction and cooling of the battery. For an accurate parameterization intensive and
L147@P2: precise measurements are necessary.
L148@P2: 3. Overview of Selected Dynamic Battery Models
L149@P2: The equivalent circuit battery model provides a generic, dynamic way of modeling Li-ion batteries
L150@P2: with moderate complexity. The moderate model complexity supports the integration of the model in
L151@P2: a multiphysical simulation, allowing to analyze dynamic effects of the electric drive train. Three models
L152@P2: are selected from the literature as the best candidates for Li-ion battery modeling, since they are the
L153@P2-3: most thorough among the reviewed models. These models are:Energies 2016, 9, 563 4 of 17
